citations.quote: This study was initially conducted during ESA's CubeSat Summer School 2024 in ESEC using a Model-Based Systems Engineering approach with the COMET tool and ESA expert support.

The first presented system analysis resulted in a 12U CubeSat design at both system and subsystem levels, including system budgets and subsystem analyses. The optical payload consisted of visible and infrared detectors aiming to observe distant celestial objects in the anti-sun direction, such as high-redshift objects, active galactic nuclei, radio galaxies and exoplanets. In the subsequent iterations, the scale-up to a micro-satellite has emerged as the optimal solution due to payload constraints.

On these premises, 'L1 Optical Lensing (LOL)' mission is carried out and aims to characterise the amplification and the resolution of the Terrascope concept by using a satellite placed at a Hill radius distance from Earth, serving both as a technological and scientific demonstration.

This paper presents a scientific and technical feasibility study that focuses on a CubeSat mission capable of demonstrating this technology. This study has been carried out by 32 students and professionals from numerous European Space Agency (ESA) member and cooperating states by following a concurrent engineering approach. The work was originally developed at the ESA CubeSat Summer School 2024.

Alongside a feasibility study of technical mission aspects, such as the Attitude and Orbit Control System (AOCS), thermal, and structural subsystems, an exploration into the scientific feasibility and utility of a Terrascope is required. A science use case is also vital in informing several subsystems, from mission analysis (to generate idealised orbits for maximum alignment) to the optical payload.

To find the rough alignment of the Terrascope exoplanet system, simulations utilising a 3-hour time step over a year-long period have been carried out with all suitable exoplanet candidates for this mission. The exoplanet catalogue used in these simulations was the NASA Exoplanet Archive, which provides 5,845 exoplanets with suitable measurements of Right Ascension (RA), Declination (DEC), and distance (at the time of access; accessible at [18]). The simulations have been run in Python, utilising the Skyfield, Astropy and Numpy libraries. If an exoplanet, at any point in the year-long run, comes within 2.5 degrees of on-axis alignment, then it is considered a potential candidate to be moved onto the next stage of analysis.
The use of the Concurrent Model-based Engineering Tool (COMET) tool, developed by ESA, has improved the workflow and accelerated the design process in its early stages [28].

By following a Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) approach, trade-offs between mission objectives, payload requirements, and subsystem requirements have been traced at an early stage, reducing the risk of late-stage redesigns.

Scientific constraints and design drivers lead, after the assessment of potential stakeholders, to the definition of high-level requirements and objectives, which will be presented throughout this section and discussed in the subsequent Space Segment section.

1. The mission shall be able to take images in the antisun direction, facing towards Earth

2. The mission shall be able to occult the Earth during the imaging frame

3. The mission shall perform nominal observation from Lagrange Point 1 (L1)

4. The spacecraft shall embark at least one NIR or IR camera

5. The mission operational lifetime shall be at least 6 months from L1 arrival

6. The mission shall be launched as a piggyback to another mission

7. The mission shall be compliant with the Space Debris Mitigation regulation
Four viable rideshare opportunities were identified, and a trade-off analysis was completed to determine which would be most beneficial.

With a launch vehicle and rideshare identified, a CONOPS was developed, which runs as follows: 1) Launch, 1.1) MECO, 2) Transfer Orbit-Insertion, 2.2) Ejection, 3) Detumbling, 4) 3x TCM, 5) Transfer Orbit, 6) STK/Orbit Stabilisation Manoeuvre, 7) In-Orbit Commissioning, 8) Operation, 9) Optional Extension, 10) EOL/Disposal into Deep Space. An example mission trajectory was simulated using Ansys STK and is shown in Figure 3.

To meet the thermal constraints, the cryocooler of the payload is positioned at the maximum possible distance from both internal heat sources and the reaction wheels, in order to mitigate thermal coupling and vibration transmission. The AOCS design (yellow in Fig. 4) included six sun sensors, one on each CubeSat face, together with two star trackers placed close to the solar panels in a shaded configuration. Attitude control relied on four reaction wheels to provide three-axis control with redundancy, complemented by two internal gyros and three magnetometers. The power subsystem (green in Fig. 4) was based on four deployable solar panels oriented towards the Sun while simultaneously shading the star tracker lenses, two secondary batteries, two On-Board Data Handling (OBDH) units, and one Power Control and Distribution Unit (PCDU).
Fig. 4. Representation of internal configuration of the 12U Terrascope satellite
citations.graphic_quote_description: Figure 4 shows the assembled and exploded 12U physical configuration. The accompanying text identifies the power subsystem in green and locates its solar panels, batteries, OBDH units, and PCDU within the spacecraft configuration.

citations.quote: At this preliminary stage, several simplifying assumptions were adopted. Component masses were only roughly estimated, and placeholder models were used that may change in dimensions and therefore do not necessarily reflect the final characteristics. No fasteners such as nuts, bolts or screws were included in the design, and neither were thermal insulation, cables, pipes or harnesses. To account for these missing elements, dedicated free volumes were reserved for the later integration of thermal insulation, electrical cabling, heaters, stand-offs, mounting plates and damping devices. This approach ensures sufficient margins for integration while enabling a first-order assessment of subsystem accommodation.

The structural design must ensure compatibility with standardised COTS dispensers. Accordingly, the platform rails and their positioning shall follow the CubeSat Design Specification (CDS) requirements, while the remaining structure can be tailored to mission-specific needs.

The Terrascope concept relies on maintaining strict alignment with the Earth's atmosphere focal line; therefore, both pointing and attitude stability requirements are derived from payload and system analyses in a concurrent way to meet the mission objectives, obtaining a balanced and efficient solution. For this mission, the pointing requirement has been established to $ \Delta\theta\approx 10^{-3} $ deg ( $ \sim $ 3.6 arcsec), which is typically orders of magnitude more stringent than the state of the art CubeSat-class missions and even comparable with space astronomical observatories.

A first-order disturbance analysis has been performed, and to support this, the selected AOCS control law is currently based on a simple Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) control law developed in MATLAB Simulink. These preliminary studies show the feasibility of meeting the pointing requirements, but a complete assessment including 6 degrees of freedom and full actuator dynamics sensor noise, jitter propagation and attitude determination algorithms combined with payload measurements remains an open point and will be the subject of further work.

The LOL satellite power subsystem is based on deployable high-efficiency solar panels and a rechargeable battery system, sized to guarantee continuous operation in theL1 orbit. The preliminary configuration considers a generation capacity in the range of 0.95 - 1.2 W per solar cell. Considering the baseline design with 2.5x6U deployable solar panels, the generation capacity of the platform is between 38W and 48W, sufficient to cover the needs of the optical payload, the cryocooler, the AOCS and communications with an additional 30% margin for contingencies.

Energy storage is provided by lithium-ion batteries with an estimated capacity of 86 Wh per unit, designed to withstand peak consumption during manoeuvres or high-rate downlink sessions. Power is distributed through a PCDU that provides regulated 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V lines, including protections and basic redundancies.

Detailed analysis of all subsystems has been carried out, all of which point towards the possibility of a future successful realisation of a Terrascope mission. However, to realistically fit all components of such a system (which requires fine pointing, its own propulsion, careful thermal management, and complex optical setups) into a 12U CubeSat is overly ambitious, and as such, increasing the size to greater than 12U would be sensible.

Future studies, taking advantage of extra space, need to be completed to explore topics not covered here. Some examples include the full assessment of the AOCS system (taking into consideration sensor noise, jitter propagation, etc), a detailed analysis of a system capable of occulting the Earth and dealing with scattered sunlight, as well as more refined Lyapunov orbits to properly account for the correct offsets as required by exoplanet alignments, to name a few.
